summary: Defines terms for a methodology that measures how fast IP routers forward packets depending on the size and makeup of their forwarding information base. It is a terminology document, not a test procedure. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Before testing how quickly a mail sorter works, everyone should agree on the words. This does that for testing how fast routers look up where to send packets.

questions: how to measure router forwarding performance
subtitle: Standard terms for testing how IP routers forward packets as their routing tables grow.

tldr.problem: When testing IP router performance, engineers needed a way to measure how fast a router forwards packets when its forwarding table grows large or has many long network prefixes.
tldr.mechanism: This memo defines standard terminology for the size and structure of a router's forwarding database, and metrics for measuring how performance changes with different table configurations.
tldr.outcome: Vendors and testers can now use a common vocabulary to compare routers fairly and to understand performance trade-offs as networks grow.

facts.label: Performance metrics
facts.value: 5 (max size, learning time, throughput, latency, frame loss)

today: RFC 3222 is informational and remains a foundation for router benchmarking. The methodology defined in related standards documents (such as RFC 2544 for network devices) uses this terminology. Modern routers continue to grow larger forwarding tables, making these metrics increasingly relevant for understanding performance trade-offs.

sections.title: The Benchmarking Problem
sections.content:
IP routers forward packets by looking up the destination address in a table and finding which output port to use. This table, called the Forwarding Information Base (FIB), can contain thousands or millions of network routes. As the internet grows, routers need larger tables, and larger tables can slow down the lookup process.

Engineers need a way to measure and compare how different routers handle large tables. Before they can do this fairly, they must agree on definitions. This memo defines the terms used to describe a router's forwarding table and the metrics for measuring performance.
sections.eli5: A router is like a mail sorter that looks at each address and decides which bin to put it in. When the sorter has more addresses to learn, sorting gets slower. This document explains the words to use when measuring how much slower.

sections.title: Forwarding Table Concepts
sections.content:
The forwarding table is built from network prefixes: contiguous blocks of bits at the start of an IP address that identify a network. For example, the prefix 192.168.0.0/24 uses the first 24 bits to identify a network, leaving 8 bits for individual hosts.

Each entry in the forwarding table contains a network prefix and the next hop (the router or interface through which packets for that network should be sent). The FIB size is the count of all entries, and the FIB prefix distribution describes how many entries use each prefix length. A distribution like {[/16, 100], [/20, 360], [/24, 540]} means 100 entries with 16-bit prefixes, 360 with 20-bit prefixes, and 540 with 24-bit prefixes.
sections.eli5: The table has rows, and each row names a block of addresses and where to send them. The memo defines the words for describing the table's size and shape.

sections.title: Router Optimizations and Their Pitfalls
sections.content:
Router makers optimize lookup performance in two ways. A per-interface FIB copies the entire table onto each router's output interface, so lookups do not have to reach the main processor. A per-interface FIB cache keeps a smaller copy of the most-used routes on each interface.

These optimizations help real-world traffic, where popular destinations are queried more often. But they complicate benchmarking: if a test uses only popular routes, a cached interface will perform better than it would with random traffic. To measure true performance, testers must spread traffic evenly across all routes, defeating the cache. The memo warns benchmarkers to account for these optimizations.
sections.eli5: Routers keep copies of the table on each output wire to speed things up. This makes real mail sort faster but can trick test results, so testers need to be careful.

sections.title: Performance Metrics
sections.content:
The memo defines five metrics for measuring FIB-based performance. Maximum FIB size is the largest table the router can hold. FIB learning time is how long it takes the router to learn and install all routes advertised to it. FIB-dependent throughput is the number of packets per second the router forwards when the table is at a given size. FIB-dependent latency is the time between receiving a packet and forwarding it. FIB-dependent frame loss is the percentage of packets the router must discard when congested.

All of these metrics can vary with the FIB size and prefix distribution. The memo's methodology requires testing at several table sizes and distributions to understand a router's real-world performance.
sections.eli5: The memo names five numbers to measure: how big a table the router can hold, how fast it learns routes, how many packets it can sort per second with a big table, how long it takes to sort one, and how many it drops when too many arrive at once.

sections.title: Controlling Unwanted Effects
sections.content:
Benchmarkers must be careful to test what they mean to test. For example, route aggregation lets a router automatically combine related routes into a single table entry, reducing table size. If a router aggregates routes, the test will not truly measure performance with the intended table size. The memo requires advertisers to send routes in a way that prevents aggregation, and to disable aggregation if possible.

Similarly, when advertising routes with a routing protocol rather than configuring them statically, engineers must ensure the routes are advertised to different interfaces to avoid aggregation.
sections.eli5: Routers can combine some routes into one to save space, which would trick the test. Testers need to prevent this to get honest results.
